title: Actors for Agents: Patterns for Production AI
gist: Manju Rajashekhar (Mad Labs, QCon AI) argues production AI agents are distributed systems in disguise and that the actor model maps one-to-one onto them, yielding five patterns (task as universal primitive, write-through state, indirect continuation, mutable execution graph, supervision boundaries). He ends with a Greenspun's-rule variant that complicated agent loops accidentally reimplement half an actor system, and backs it with a minimal Rust coding agent.

insights.claim: When an agent demo meets production, the hard part shifts from reasoning and prompts to runtime: slow tool calls, rate limits, follow-up questions mid-run, and worker restarts.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Agent reliability is an infrastructure problem; investment shifts toward runtime and orchestration layers.
insights.locator: Suddenly the hard part is no longer about the reasoning

insights.claim: Production changes four things: time (a function call is a poor abstraction for work that returns later), interaction (users ask follow-ups while the agent runs), delegation (execution becomes a tree or graph), and failure (exceptions become normal operating conditions).
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Request-response architectures are mismatched to agentic workloads.
insights.locator: The first thing that changes is this notion of time.

insights.claim: Agent systems grow sideways because chat, workflow state, queues, databases and retry state live in different places with no single execution model, so recovery becomes a second implementation of the workload.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Fragmented state across components is a source of hard-to-debug agent failures.
insights.locator: At this point, because the production changed the shape of the problem

insights.claim: Production agents are distributed systems in disguise: stateful, concurrent, long-running, communicating, failing in parts and restarting independently.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Distributed-systems expertise transfers to agent engineering.
insights.quote: the production agents are just distributed systems in disguise
insights.locator: The moment we start looking at production agents as a runtime problem

insights.claim: Erlang and OTP made actor thinking operational, with a system of over 2 million lines of Erlang code available for 20 years at nine nines of availability.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Actor-based runtimes have a track record for extreme reliability that agent systems want to borrow.
insights.locator: It is Erlang and OTP that made the actor style thinking operational

insights.claim: The actor model replaces the question of who may mutate shared state with which actor owns the state: only the owner changes it and others send messages, avoiding locks, mutexes and defensive copying.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Clear state ownership simplifies consistency in concurrent systems.
insights.locator: This leads us to the first foundational design principle of an actor

insights.claim: Because everything is a message, senders and receivers are loosely coupled, execution is sequential inside an actor and concurrent across actors, so the model puts boundaries around concurrency rather than removing it.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Message passing enables local reasoning about concurrent systems.
insights.locator: I want all of you guys to pause on this principle

insights.claim: Failure has a boundary in the actor model through supervision, where a supervisor can restart, stop, or escalate to a human or system with partial results, making failure an architectural concern.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Failure policy at architecture level beats scattered try-catch and retry code.
insights.locator: Then the final foundational principle with the actor model

insights.claim: An agent task actor owns the goal, context, tools in flight and child tasks, and all events (user messages, tool results, follow-ups like 'include Europe') arrive as messages through a single mailbox rather than separate chat, workflow and cancellation pathways.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: A unified mailbox removes side channels and simplifies agent control flow.
insights.locator: Now, take this order actor and replace it with an agent task actor.

insights.claim: Actor identity maps to a durable handle for running work, child actors map to delegated subtasks, tool calls or specialist agents, and supervision maps to failure boundaries, making agents actor-shaped.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: The mapping supports using actor runtimes for agents.
insights.locator: Child actors map to delegated subtasks

insights.claim: Pattern one: the task becomes the universal execution primitive, so chat, workflows, tool calls, delegated subproblems and waiting for human input all share the same contract of identity, mailbox, state, lifecycle and supervision.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: One runtime contract replaces fragmented chat, job and workflow systems.
insights.locator: The first pattern is that the task becomes the universal execution primitive.

insights.claim: Pattern two: write-through state makes every meaningful state transition durable as messages are processed, so crash recovery is the same path as normal resumption by rehydrating the actor.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Unified recovery and resumption cuts failure-handling code and bugs.
insights.locator: The second pattern that follows through is write-through state.

insights.claim: Pattern three: indirect continuation records the task's intent instead of preserving a blocked call stack, so waiting minutes or until a human responds tomorrow costs no pinned thread.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Long-horizon waits require intent-based state, not stack-based state.
insights.locator: The third pattern that follows from this is what I call as the indirect continuation.

insights.claim: Pattern four: a mutable execution graph, because unlike a static DAG workflow, agents discover steps while executing, so the runtime must represent the evolving structure of work.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Static workflow engines fit agents poorly.
insights.locator: The fourth pattern that follows through is this thing called the mutable execution graph.

insights.claim: Pattern five: supervision boundaries give failures a policy (restart, retry, escalate, keep partial results, ask the user), making failure a local event instead of a global concern.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Failure policy per subtree improves reliability of nondeterministic agent systems.
insights.locator: Failure policy becomes a structural concern

insights.claim: The actor model will not make agents easy to build; it makes the hard parts explicit and named, since production AI builds correct execution on a non-deterministic LLM foundation with unreliable external systems.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Expect no silver bullet; value is in clearer boundaries.
insights.quote: the actor model is not going to make your agents easy to build
insights.locator: A good question to ask here is, what is the payoff

insights.claim: Rajashekhar proposes a five-question design checklist: what are the actors, what state does each own, what messages do they exchange, what can fail independently, and who supervises whom.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: A framework-agnostic review checklist for agent architecture.
insights.locator: Ask these five questions

insights.claim: A minimal Rust coding agent has four actors (supervisor, LLM, tool registry, agent), connects to local models like Qwen, OpenAI or Anthropic models, and is meant as a teaching artifact.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Shows actor design for coding agents in practice, though not production proven.
insights.locator: The code that I'm going to share here, is just a minimal coding agent.

insights.claim: Rajashekhar's Greenspun's-rule variant states that any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains an ad hoc, informally specified, bug-ridden implementation of half of an actor system, so teams build actor-shaped systems either accidentally or intentionally.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Agent frameworks are likely to converge on actor-like runtimes.
insights.quote: any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains an ad hoc, informally specified, bug-ridden implementation of half of an actor system
insights.locator: Let me end the talk with a variation of Greenspun's 10th rule.

insights.claim: Rajashekhar hypothesises actors are absent from coding agents because Python and TypeScript dominate and the model needs a robust runtime, so agent frameworks rediscover pieces of it in a half-baked way; he sees no existing framework to plug it into and notes Erlang/BEAM and agents have not yet met.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Gap for runtimes like BEAM or Rust actor frameworks in agent infrastructure.
insights.locator: This is just a hypothesis, but part of the reasoning

insights.claim: When one agent must pass large context to another, the context is sent as messages (by copy or pointer to a copy) and the owner keeps the state; he argues LLM token processing time dominates the cost over moving the data.
insights.speaker: Manju Rajashekhar
insights.so_what: Context transfer cost is secondary to token processing latency in agent design.
insights.locator: The context still gets sent as messages.
